title: Evidence and Surveillance Admissibility: When Watching Becomes Proof
body:
The admissibility of surveillance evidence in GLMZ's court systems is governed by a framework so fragmented that experienced attorneys describe it less as law and more as 'a negotiation you have every time.' The central statute is the Meridian Evidence Integrity Code of 2169, which established standards for the admissibility of digital, biometric, and neural interface data in criminal and civil proceedings. The Code was designed for a surveillance landscape that was already dense in 2169 and has since expanded by orders of magnitude — meaning its provisions are applied to data types and collection methods its drafters never anticipated, often by stretching definitional language to its breaking point.

The most consequential provision of the Evidence Integrity Code is Section 14, which governs 'passive collection data' — surveillance gathered without active targeting of a specific individual. Under Section 14, passive collection data is presumptively admissible in criminal proceedings without a warrant, provided the collection system was operating within a licensed surveillance zone. As of 2199, 94% of Meridian's public and semi-public spaces are designated licensed surveillance zones, including all transit infrastructure, all commercial districts, and all public green spaces. The practical effect is that a person's movements, behavioral patterns, and — through licensed BCI network monitoring — certain categories of neural data can be used against them in court without any prior judicial authorization.

ACJ evidence presents a separate set of problems. Data collected within Autonomous Corporate Jurisdictions by the corponation's own surveillance systems is subject to the host corponation's Charter of Operations rather than the Evidence Integrity Code. This data can be introduced in Meridian Civic Court proceedings only if the corponation chooses to share it — which it does selectively. In practice, ACJ surveillance data is shared when it supports the corponation's interests and withheld when it does not, with no legal mechanism to compel disclosure in most cases. Defense attorneys have documented numerous cases in which exculpatory ACJ footage was withheld in corponation-involved prosecutions; the standard judicial response is that the court lacks jurisdiction to compel ACJ data disclosure.

Neural interface data admissibility is governed by a 2183 amendment to the Evidence Integrity Code called the Cognitive Record Provision, which allows 'verified neural recordings' — data authenticated by the interface manufacturer — to be used as evidence of intent, memory, or emotional state in criminal proceedings. The Provision has generated sustained controversy because the authentication process is controlled by the same manufacturers who produce and maintain the interfaces, creating an obvious conflict of interest. In the 2196 murder case People of Meridian v. Farida Nazari, the prosecution introduced authenticated neural recordings that the defense argued had been algorithmically reconstructed from fragmentary data — a process that NeuroFrame Ltd., the authenticating manufacturer, acknowledged in internal documents released through a separate civil proceeding. Nazari was convicted; her appeal citing the Cognitive Record Provision's authentication standards is currently before the Meridian Circuit Appellate Panel.
